title: MotionMAR: Multi-scale Motion Reconstruction from Sparse Tracking Data
one_liner: Build human motion from partial tracking data by reconstructing from coarse shape first, then adding fine details.
lead: When you have only a few markers tracking a human body (like wrists and ankles), filling in the missing joints is hard because the full shape can bend many ways. MotionMAR rebuilds motion in layers: first it recovers the overall body trajectory and pose, then it gradually adds in the fine wiggles and natural smoothness. This mimics how humans actually move—big gestures first, details follow.

problem.h2: Sparse motion capture loses too much information
paras: Tracking human motion with only a few markers (wrists, ankles, head) leaves most of the body unseen. To fill in the missing joints, you have to guess what the torso, elbows, knees, and fingers are doing based only on where the endpoints landed.

A naive approach: take the positions you have and fit them to a pose model that predicts everything else at once. This fails because the intermediate parts can fit many different poses to the same sparse observations. The system gets confused and produces jerky, unrealistic motion with sudden jumps or twisted limbs.

The real issue is that human motion has structure: the body first moves as a whole unit (the global trajectory and spine), then the limbs add variations on top. Flat, one-shot pose fitting ignores this hierarchy.

callout.html: Reconstruct motion in layers, starting with the overall shape and then gradually refining in the details.

steps.text: Feed the real motion into an encoder that breaks it into multiple time-scales (every frame, every-other frame, every-four-frames), creating a tree of motion descriptors from coarse to fine.
Convert each layer into discrete symbols (like words in a dictionary), so the generator can predict one symbol at a time, building motion sequentially instead of all at once.
A neural network starts with the coarsest layer (roughest shape), using attention (a mechanism that focuses on relevant pieces of input) to predict what comes next based on sparse marker positions.
Working from coarse to fine, each layer refines what came before, adding more joints and more detail at every step.
A refinement network smooths out quantization artifacts (rough edges from the discrete codes) and enforces that the sparse markers stay pinned to their true positions.

paras: MotionMAR changes how motion is predicted: instead of guessing all joints at once from sparse markers, it builds motion in layers, starting with a coarse outline and filling in details.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: multi-scale motion codes
hidden.name: temporal hierarchy (coarse-to-fine layers)
paras: Human motion is not random jitter. It has natural layers: large body swings happen slowly (coarse), while hand jitter and foot shuffles happen quickly (fine). The paper measures where each motion component 'lives' in this hierarchy by encoding motion at different time-scales (every frame, every 2 frames, every 4 frames). Each scale produces a set of discrete motion codes (like a vocabulary of poses).

The paper estimates this hierarchy using a multi-scale VQ-VAE (a compression algorithm that learns motion patterns at each scale). At training time, it passes real motion through this encoder and watches which codes activate at each scale. At test time, it uses these learned code patterns to guide reconstruction from sparse markers.

heat.caption: Darker means coarser structure; each scale learns its own vocabulary of motion patterns.

reads.html: The hierarchy is simply that some motion happens on large time scales (the body takes 2 seconds to turn) and some on fast ones (fingers twitch every frame).
The Temporal Multi-scale VQ-VAE (a compression algorithm) learns separate discrete codes for each time resolution, separating semantic motion (coarse) from jitter (fine).

paras: The mechanism is simple: the big pose is easier to infer from sparse markers than all the details are. When you know your wrists and ankles, you can guess your torso and spine pretty reliably. Once the skeleton backbone is fixed, predicting the remaining fine poses becomes a much smaller search problem.

A neural network operates on discrete motion codes, predicting one time-scale at a time. Starting with the coarsest layer (big body shape every few frames), it uses attention (a focus mechanism) to generate which pose code comes next, conditioned on the sparse marker positions. Then it zooms in to finer time-scales, refining the shape it already committed to. This is more stable than trying to solve for all joints at once, because earlier layers constrain later ones—the backbone is locked in, so the fingers can only jiggle within that constraint.

The scale-aware control module acts as a global anchor: it ensures the generated skeleton still touches the sparse markers at the observed frames. A refinement network then smooths the result and removes discrete artifacts.

math.words: For each time-scale layer, compare the predicted discrete motion code against the true code at that scale, using cross-entropy loss (penalizing wrong predictions). The total loss sums these penalties across all scales, weighted by learned importance factors.
math.equation: L_total = sum_k ( lambda_k * cross_entropy( predicted_codes_k, true_codes_k ) )
symbols: the discrete motion symbols the network predicts at scale k
the correct symbols extracted from real motion at scale k
learned weight for how much each scale matters
a measure of how wrong the prediction is (0 if perfect, high if very wrong)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Real motion at scale 1 (coarse): body at code 5 (standing pose). Network predicts code 5. Cross-entropy loss: 0 (correct).
Real motion at scale 2 (medium): left arm at code 12 (raised). Network predicts code 8 (lowered). Cross-entropy loss: 2.1 (wrong).
Real motion at scale 3 (fine): finger jitter at code 3. Network predicts code 3. Cross-entropy loss: 0 (correct).
Total loss for this frame: lambda_1 * 0 + lambda_2 * 2.1 + lambda_3 * 0 = 2.1 * lambda_2. If lambda_2 = 1.0, total = 2.1.

math.note: The network learns to predict one layer at a time, with each error penalized according to its scale's importance weight.

charts.title: Naive one-shot method
charts.note: Tries to fit all joints at once; produces jerky, inaccurate motion.

charts.title: MotionMAR (coarse-to-fine)
charts.note: Layered reconstruction keeps intermediate joints realistic and smooth throughout.

items.b: Rare motions or highly ambiguous cases fail.
items.html: When the sparse markers don't uniquely determine the pose (e.g., hand positions that could belong to multiple arm configs), the method can still pick the wrong one if the training data never saw that posture. Physics-based priors (e.g., joint angle limits) would eliminate impossible poses, leaving only realistic ones to choose from, but MotionMAR learns only from data and doesn't encode these hard constraints.

The motion vocabulary has finite size, so some true motion patterns may not have a close match. The network predicts the nearest code, which can make motion snap or feel slightly unnatural at code boundaries.
If the smoothing and artifact-removal network is undertrained, the output can still look jerky despite the coarse-to-fine strategy.

items.b: Done right: multimodal ambiguity is broken early.
items.html: By committing to a coarse shape first, the network eliminates many false alternatives before they can accumulate errors in finer layers. Each layer refines what came before, not starting from scratch.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a demo that takes a video or motion file with full-body ground truth but artificially masks out all but four joints (head, two hands, two feet). Then feed only the sparse markers to MotionMAR and measure how well it reconstructs the hidden joints. Compare three pipelines: (1) a flat neural network that predicts all joints from sparse markers at once, (2) the hierarchical coarse-to-fine prediction without the refinement network, and (3) the full MotionMAR with all layers and smoothing.
demo.metric_eq: reconstruction_error = average distance between predicted and true joint positions (in cm)
demo.closing: The demo must show that coarse-first prediction produces lower error than flat one-shot fitting, and that the full pipeline (with refinement) is smoother to watch as a video.
